Testimony ofRep. Sally Cluchey presenting
LD 329, An Act to Increase the Fine for Passing a Stopped School Bus
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Transportation
Good morning, Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and honorable members of the Transportation
Committee. My name is Sally Cluchey, and I represent House District 52, which includes the communities of Bowdoinham, Bowdoin, and Richmond. I'm here to present LD 329: An Act to Increase
the Fine for Passing a Stopped School Bus.
This bill was brought to me by Katie Spear, a Richmond resident and the Transportation Director for
RSU2, whose drivers see firsthand how often this happens. It's also a recurring problem in MSAD 75
and other rural districts, where young children -- sometimes as young as five --- are crossing the road
alone.
At my request, Sagadahoc County Sheriff Joel Merry gathered data from all law enforcement agencies
in Sagadahoc county. In just over two years, there were 143 complaints about this violation. Only 8
resulted in criminal summonses, 3 in civil citations, and ll in warnings -- about 15% enforcement. I want to emphasize: this is not a reflection of law enforcement failing to do their jobs. I am deeply
grateful to Sheriff Merry and to every officer who works to keep our roads safe. Enforcement is
extremely difficult and time-consuming. Officers often rely on secondhand reports or unclear bus
camera footage. The burden of proof for prosecution is high. And these cases, even when they're prosecuted, rarely lead to meaningful consequences for the driver. And yet the consequences for the
child can be life-changing.
Two weeks ago in the Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services Corrnnittee, we heard from a
parent whose 13-year-old son, Nathaniel, was hit by a truck that passed his stopped school bus. His lower leg and foot were crushed. He spent months in recovery, and his leg will never be the same. His
medical bills total nearly $200,000.
The challenge we're faced with here is that our laws are insufficient to deter this behavior. Maine law currently provides two different enforcement paths:
0 A civil violation with a fine of $154, and
District 52: Bowdoinham, Richmond and Bowdoin (part)

0 A criminal offense, which is a Class E crime carrying a minimum fine of $250 and a 30-day
license suspension for a second offense. Despite these penalties, this is a law that is broken frequently. This is not a crime of necessity or desperation. It's reckless, impatient, and a blatant disregard for the law that keeps our children safe.
As currently written, LD 329 increases the fine for the criminal offense. But as the data shows, most of these violations are either not charged or are charged at the civil level -- where the fine is just $154. If
this committee is open to it, I would respectfully suggest that we consider increasing the civil fine to $1,000 as well, so that the law sends a consistent and serious message regardless of how the offense is
ultimately charged.
And I'll close with this thought: Later today, this committee will be hearing several bills related to
driver 's education. I urge you to think of this bill in that same context. This is not just about penalties.
It's also about creating a culture of safety and responsibility on our roads -- starting with how we train
drivers and reinforced by how we hold them accountable.
Thank you for your time, and I welcome any questions.

TESTIMONY IN SUPPORT OF
L.D. 329
AN ACT TO INCREASE THE FINE FOR PASSING A STOPPED SCHOOL BUS
April 22, 2025
Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and esteemed members of the Transportation Committee, I am Steven Bailey, Executive Director of the Maine School Management Association, testifying on behalf of the legislative committees of the Maine School Boards Association and the Maine School Superintendents Association in strong support for L.D. 329, which proposes increasing the minimum fine for illegally passing a stopped school bus from $250 to $1,000. This legislation is a crucial step toward enhancing the safety of our children and reinforcing the seriousness of this traffic violation.
In just one single day during the 2018-2019 school year, Maine reported 173 instances of vehicles illegally passing school buses. This alarming statistic underscores the urgency of implementing effective measures to protect students. News Center Maine
Recognizing the severity of this issue, Maine passed Senate Bill 166 in 2019, legalizing the use of school bus stop-arm cameras statewide. This legislation allows school districts to install cameras on school buses to identify and penalize motorists who disregard the stop-arm signal, thereby enhancing enforcement and deterrence. busboss.com
The National Association of State Directors of Pupil Transportation Services (NASDPTS) has highlighted the prevalence of illegal passing nationwide, with over 43 million instances reported annually. This data emphasizes the need for robust enforcement measures, such as stop-arm cameras, to ensure the safety of students.
Increasing the fine for illegally passing a stopped school bus is a necessary and effective measure to protect our children. By aligning with national best practices and heeding expert recommendations, Maine can take a significant step toward ensuring the safety of students traveling to and from school.
I urge the committee to pass L.D. 329 and send a clear message that the safety of our children is paramount.
